title: Slowing light to bicycle speed
hook: In 1999 a Harvard team slowed light to about 17 metres per second.
peek: Light normally covers about 300,000 kilometres every second. In 1999 the physicist Lene Hau and her team slowed a pulse of it to roughly the speed of a fast cyclist, by sending it through a cloud of atoms colder than anywhere in nature.
lede: In empty space light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. Glass or water slow it a little, but only by a third or so. In 1999 the Danish physicist Lene Hau and her team at Harvard slowed a pulse of laser light to about 17 metres per second, around 60 kilometres an hour. A cyclist sprinting downhill could have kept pace.

bullets.text: The light passed through a tiny cloud of sodium atoms cooled to a fraction of a millionth of a degree above absolute zero. At that temperature the atoms form a Bose-Einstein condensate, a state where they act together in a single quantum state.

Normally that cloud would absorb the light completely. A second laser, shone in from the side, made it transparent to the first beam in a narrow band of colours. Inside that window the light's speed drops dramatically.
As the front of the pulse slowed on entering the cloud, the back caught up, so the pulse was squashed from about a kilometre long in the air to a fraction of a millimetre inside the atoms.
In 2001 Hau's group went further and brought a light pulse to a full stop, storing its information in the atoms. Switching the side laser back on released the pulse, which carried on its way.
